input: What the current position shows, when all of the moving parts are considered together, is a completion date that has slipped and a plan that has not yet absorbed the slip. The overrun stands at 6 weeks, and it did not arise from a general loss of momentum across the whole project. Fabrication and delivery of the main equipment package finished late, and every activity that depended on that package moved with it. Work planned against delivered equipment waited, while the work that could proceed without the package was, in practice, too small to absorb the crews released by the delay. The EPC forecast now carries the overrun in the completion date itself rather than in float, because the float on the affected chain has already been used. Against that background, the proposal placed before the project board is a single mitigation: the remaining installation work is resequenced around the delayed package, so that activities with no dependence on the package move forward and the installation crews take those activities in place of the waiting work. It should be said plainly that resequencing does not recover the full overrun, since part of the delay sits in activities that cannot begin before the package arrives, and no rearrangement of later work can remove that part. What the mitigation does is limit further loss, at the cost of managerial attention and a tighter set of interfaces between activities, because resequenced work starts with less slack than the original plan allowed. The sequence, once changed, is also the basis on which progress is reported, so that the waiting work is shown as waiting and not as slow work. The board, as owner of the mitigation, reviews the resequenced plan at each status meeting and holds the sequence unless a further delay changes the order in which the activities depend on one another.
target: Recovery of the 6 weeks is not available from the remaining installation work as it stands. Fabrication and delivery of the main equipment package finished late, and every dependent installation activity moved with the package. Work planned against delivered equipment waited, and the work that could proceed without the package was too small to absorb the crews released by the delay. The EPC forecast now carries the overrun in the completion date rather than in float, because the float on the affected chain has been used. The project board holds the one mitigation proposed here. Remaining installation work is resequenced around the delayed package: activities that do not depend on the package move forward, and the installation crews take those activities in place of the waiting work. Resequencing does not recover the full overrun. Part of the delay sits in activities that cannot start before the package arrives, and no rearrangement of later work removes that part. The mitigation limits further loss rather than restoring the original date. Its cost is managerial attention and a tighter interface between activities, because resequenced work starts with less slack than the original plan allowed. A further slip in the package would consume the remaining slack in the resequenced activities first, and the completion date would move again by the amount of that slip. The board reviews the resequenced plan at each status meeting and holds the sequence unless a further delay changes the order of dependence between activities. The resequencing also changes how the remaining work is reported. Activities moved forward are reported against their new positions, and the waiting activities are reported as waiting, with the package named as the cause. Reporting the position in that form keeps the overrun visible as a delivery problem rather than letting it dissolve into general slippage across the installation programme. No other mitigation is proposed in this part of the memo, and no recovery is claimed beyond the limit stated.
